claims.claim: Plain logistic regression at 2.4% prevalence: threshold 0.1 gave precision 0.36, recall 0.42; threshold 0.02 gave recall 0.63, precision 0.04; balanced weights at 0.5 gave recall 0.64, precision 0.05.
claims.source: Run with scikit-learn 1.9.1 in this repository (make_classification, random_state=0).

concept_html:
Imbalance. When positives are rare, a model trained as usual predicts low probabilities, and the default 0.5 threshold flags almost nothing. That is a threshold problem, not always a model problem.

In this course's build (2.4% positives, logistic regression, scikit-learn 1.8), the plain model at 0.5 flagged 3 cases and found none. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 flagged 284 cases with precision 0.36 and recall 0.42. At 0.02 it reached recall 0.63 with precision 0.04. The same model trained with class_weight="balanced" reached recall 0.64 and precision 0.05 at 0.5: a very similar trade-off, with probabilities that were no longer calibrated (lesson B12-L2).

Options, in the order to try them:

  1. Train normally and choose the threshold from capacity or cost (lesson B12-L1). Probabilities stay calibrated.
  2. Class weights when the model struggles to learn the minority class at all. Recalibrate afterwards if you need probabilities.
  3. Resampling (over- or under-sampling) inside the training folds only. Never resample the test set: its class balance must match production.

Error analysis. One overall metric hides where a model fails. Break the test results down by segment: region, device, customer tenure, survey mode. For each segment report the count, positives, precision and recall. A model with recall 0.60 overall can have recall 0.15 for new customers, the group the campaign most wants to reach.

Then read examples. Take the 20 most confident false positives and the 20 most confident false negatives, and look at them with someone who knows the domain. Patterns in those 40 rows often point to a missing feature, a label error or a leak.

Report segment results with their counts. A recall of 0.20 from 5 positives is a question, not a finding.

lines: import pandas as pd
def metrics_by_segment(df: pd.DataFrame, segment: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Count, positives, precision and recall per segment. Columns y and flagged are 0/1."""
rows = []
for name, g in df.groupby(segment, sort=True):
tp = int(((g["y"] == 1) & (g["flagged"] == 1)).sum())
n_flag, n_pos = int(g["flagged"].sum()), int(g["y"].sum())
rows.append({
segment: name,
"n": len(g),
"positives": n_pos,
"precision": tp / n_flag if n_flag > 0 else None,
"recall": tp / n_pos if n_pos > 0 else None,
})
return pd.DataFrame(rows)

import pandas as pd


def metrics_by_segment(df: pd.DataFrame, segment: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Count, positives, precision and recall per segment.

    Args:
        df: Columns y and flagged (0/1) plus the segment column.
        segment: Name of the segment column.

    Returns:
        One row per segment, sorted by segment.
    """
    rows = []
    for name, g in df.groupby(segment, sort=True):
        tp = int(((g["y"] == 1) & (g["flagged"] == 1)).sum())
        n_flag = int(g["flagged"].sum())
        n_pos = int(g["y"].sum())
        rows.append(
            {
                segment: name,
                "n": len(g),
                "positives": n_pos,
                "precision": tp / n_flag if n_flag > 0 else None,
                "recall": tp / n_pos if n_pos > 0 else None,
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

code_lines: import pandas as pd
def prepare_sets(train: pd.DataFrame, test: pd.DataFrame, seed: int) -> tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.DataFrame]:
"""Oversample positives so the model sees more of them."""
pos_train = train[train["y"] == 1].sample(frac=5.0, replace=True, random_state=seed)
pos_test = test[test["y"] == 1].sample(frac=5.0, replace=True, random_state=seed)
return pd.concat([train, pos_train]), pd.concat([test, pos_test])

title: Imbalanced classes and error analysis by segment
why_html: A complaint-routing model reported recall 0.71 overall. Complaints arriving by the new web chat were 18% of the volume and had recall 0.22: the model had been trained mostly on email text, and chat messages were shorter and informal. Urgent chat complaints waited in the general queue for three weeks before a supervisor noticed. A per-channel breakdown at validation would have shown it.
